newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk auto industry says more job losses probable.
newsitem.headline: Turk auto industry says more job losses probable.

text.p: Between 4,000 and 5,000 job losses in Turkey's automotive parts industry could occur due to sharp drops in domestic car sales amid expectations of cheaper car imports following a recent decree easing import rules, the automotive industry association (OSD) said.

"The government's insistence on allowing (limited) duty free imports has affected the car market very negatively. Although the number of applications for the scheme seem few for now, the expectation (of cheaper imports) has reduced sales sharply," OSD chairman Ali Ihsan Ilkbahar said in a statement on Wednesday.

"After hearing (leading car maker) Tofas's decision to reduce its production to single shift from two and the loss of around 1,000 jobs, the probability of another 4,000 to 5,000 losing their jobs in the related parts industry has made us deeply worried," Ilkbahar said.

Tofas Turk Otomobil Fabrikasi equally owned by Italian Fiat Spa and Koc Holding would lay off 1,011 workers or 22 percent of its workforce on January 2, 1997, an official from labour union Turk Metal told Reuters.

The union's Bursa branch where Tofas's plant is located, said an agreement in principle was reached with the company to put the 1,011 workers on compulsory leave with half pay from November 22 to January 2, 1997.

The OSD said Turkey's five car plants already operated at one third of their capacity due to low demand. Sales of locally produced cars fell 8.5 percent to 139,829 in January-October 1996 when compared to the same 1995 period.

A cabinet decree taking effect on October 24 allows three million expatriate Turkish workers in Europe to import cars and machinery of up to four years of age without customs duties, if they deposit a minimum of 50,000 marks ($33,100) for one year at state-owned Ziraat Bank.

Expatriates who open the minimum account by end-1996 will be allowed to bring in one duty free foreign car or 50,000 German marks worth of machinery from June 1, 1997. They will also receive 10 percent annual interest on their deposits.
The Anatolian agency reported on Wednesday that such accounts totalling 42 million marks had so far been opened.
Turkey's car output plunged 32 percent from a year ago to 17,350 units in October and fell by seven percent to 172,964 in January-October when compared to the same 1995 period.
The government forecasts 25,000 duty free car imports and an income of 1.25 billion marks in 1997 from the scheme as part of its two revenue raising packages unveiled since late July.

Car sales in the first ten months of 1996 rose by 8.12 percent to 178,618 from the same 1995 period, but the OSD said this increase was entirely due to a sharp rise in imported car sales which tripled to 38,789 over this period.
-- Aydan Eksin, Istanbul newsroom +90-212-2750875 ($ = 1.506 German Marks)
